To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
In Still's disease, AGP and ACT microheterogeneity and serum ferritin and ACT concentration differ significantly in children and adults.

1) the microheterogeneous forms of AGP and ACT in sera of patients are altered in the same manner as in sera of patients suffering from chronic inflammation, 2) the reactivity of both glycoproteins in sera of patients is increased in adult and decreased in child-onset disease, and 3) ACT and ferritin are of value as a marker for the adult but not for the juvenile form of the disease.
the reactivity of AGP and ACT with Con A was increased in sera from adults with Still's disease, while it was decreased in sera from children with Still's disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the microheterogeneous pattern of AGP and ACT and with the concentration of ferritin, ACT, and AGP in sera of children and adults with Still's disease.
the microheterogeneous structure of glycoproteins and their clinical significance in the diagnosis and differential diagnosis of Still's disease.
the microheterogeneous pattern of AGP and ACT in the sera of children and adults with Still's disease, as well as with their possible use as markers of the activity of the disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the adult and juvenile forms of Still's disease are different diseases.
the pattern of acute-phase protein response in Still's disease is not uniform, and that the pattern of response is different in the two age groups.
the pathophysiological mechanisms in the juvenile form of the disease are not identical to those in the adult form.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pattern of acute-phase protein changes is not the same in Still's disease in adults and children.
the microheterogeneous forms of AGP and ACT could be useful as markers for monitoring disease activity in Still's disease.

adult Still's disease is characterized by an increased level of acute-phase proteins, including ACT and AGP, and by a decrease in the concentration of ferritin, while juvenile Still's disease is marked by an increase of ferritin, but not by an increase of acute-phase proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown that the pattern of acute-phase reactants is different in children and adults with Still's disease, suggesting that the pathogenesis of the two diseases is also different.
the microheterogeneous pattern of ACT and AGP in sera of patients could be used as a marker for adult and juvenile Still's disease, respectively.
we have found that the reactivity of both AGP and ACT is increased in adult-onset Still’s disease, but decreased in child-onset disease.
